title: Design ride-hailing (Uber/Lyft) with geospatial matching
relevance: High — flagship HLD question (campus + experienced) at Uber, Lyft, Ola, Grab, FAANG, Flipkart/Swiggy-style product cos; probes real-time geo index + matching consistency.
company_notes: Campus/new-grad: Uber/Ola/Swiggy HLD and FAANG “design Uber/nearby drivers” — Redis GEO + basic matching, light estimation. Experienced (1–4+ YOE): H3 vs geohash, batch vs greedy, lock TTL, city sharding, ETA/surge, queue durability at Uber, Lyft, Grab, Meta/Google geo loops, Flipkart logistics. Among the highest-signal classic HLD prompts; often paired with proximity/Yelp as the static twin of the same geo toolkit.

phases.goal: Lock matching + location scope, NFRs, and metro-first assumptions before designing.

must_hit.point: Functional in-scope: fare estimate for pickup+destination; request ride and match a nearby available driver; driver accept/decline and navigate pickup→dropoff; continuous driver location updates with rider ETA / approaching-car view.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists fare estimate, match nearby driver, accept/decline+navigate, and live location/ETA as the core loop.

must_hit.point: Park payments, ratings, scheduled rides, multi-hop pool, and fraud unless probed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly marks those as out of scope / below the line unless the interviewer asks.

must_hit.point: NFRs: match in seconds (often < ~30–60s to match or fail); strong consistency on assignment (one driver ↔ one active trip); survive city-scale spikes; location freshness on the order of a few seconds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States seconds-scale match latency (~30–60s bound), assignment consistency, spike survival, and few-second location freshness.

must_hit.point: State assumptions aloud: one metro first; global = many independent city shards; vehicle types later.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Scopes to one metro initially and treats global as city shards, deferring vehicle types.

probes: What is in scope for this ride-hailing design, what is out, and what match-latency / consistency NFRs are you assuming?

hints.1: Start with matching + location, then ask what to cut.
hints.2: Separate top functional flows from NFRs and metro-first assumptions.
hints.3: In: fare, request/match, accept/decline+navigate, live location/ETA; out: payments/ratings/scheduled/pool/fraud; NFRs: ~30–60s match, strong assignment consistency, few-second location freshness; one metro then city shards.

phases.goal: Show city-shard driver pings dominate write QPS and force an in-memory geo index off the OLTP path.

must_hit.point: Fleet scale: ~1–5M concurrent online drivers globally; a city shard might be 50k–200k online.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States ~1–5M global online drivers and 50k–200k as a city-shard working set.

must_hit.point: Ping every 3–5 s → city write QPS ≈ drivers / 4 (e.g. 100k drivers → ~25k GEO writes/s).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Derives city GEO write QPS from 3–5 s pings as drivers/4, citing ~25k/s for 100k drivers.

must_hit.point: Ride requests are much smaller (hundreds–low thousands RPS peak per large city); nearby/map queries are 5–10× requests.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts request RPS (hundreds–low thousands) with 5–10× nearby/map amplification.

must_hit.point: Hot path is the Redis working set (current lat/lng + status); historical GPS goes Kafka → cold store — not on the match path; OLTP DB cannot be the geo index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Puts current location in Redis and parks history on Kafka/cold store, rejecting OLTP as the geo index.

probes: How many GEO writes/s does a large city produce from driver pings, and why can’t OLTP own that index?

hints.1: Estimate city online drivers and ping interval first.
hints.2: Write QPS ≈ drivers / 4; compare to much smaller ride-request RPS.
hints.3: 50k–200k city online; ping 3–5 s → e.g. 100k → ~25k GEO writes/s; requests hundreds–low thousands RPS; Redis working set vs Kafka cold history.

phases.goal: Define fare/ride/location/offer endpoints plus push channels without trusting client identity or fare amounts.

must_hit.point: POST /fares (pickup, destination, optional product) → fareId/estimate/eta; POST /rides with fareId → rideId status REQUESTED (matching async).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows fare estimate then async ride create returning REQUESTED.

must_hit.point: POST /drivers/location for GPS updates; PATCH /rides/:rideId with ACCEPT|DECLINE; GET ride status and/or WebSocket push; GET /drivers/nearby for map pins with fuzzed positions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers location write, accept/decline, status read/push, and fuzzed nearby pins.

must_hit.point: Auth via JWT/session — never trust client-sent driverId or fare amount; push offers to drivers and location/status to riders.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects client-owned driverId/fareAmount and names push for offers and rider updates.

probes: Walk the APIs for fare estimate, request ride, driver location, and accept/decline — what must the server own?

hints.1: Separate fare snapshot, async ride create, and location write.
hints.2: Add accept/decline + push; never trust client driverId/fare.
hints.3: POST /fares → POST /rides (REQUESTED async); POST /drivers/location; PATCH ACCEPT|DECLINE; push offer/location; fuzz nearby; JWT owns identity.

phases.goal: Split hot DriverLocation geo state from durable Fare/Ride SQL entities and a strict ride status machine.

must_hit.point: Hot DriverLocation (driverId, lat, lng, cellId, updatedAt, status) lives in Redis; SQL/DocStore holds Rider/Driver profiles, Fare estimate snapshots, and Ride rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Puts who-is-free-where-now in Redis and rides/fares/users in SQL.

must_hit.point: Ride status: REQUESTED | OFFERED | ACCEPTED | EN_ROUTE | IN_TRIP | COMPLETED | CANCELLED; illegal transitions must be impossible; optional Offer (rideId, driverId, expiresAt) for audit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those statuses as a state machine and may mention Offer for audit.

must_hit.point: Geo index shape: Redis GEO key per city (member=driverId) or Redis SET drivers:h3:{cellId} plus hash driver:{id} metadata.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names either Redis GEO per city or H3 cell sets + driver hashes.

probes: What lives in Redis versus SQL, and what are the ride status transitions?

hints.1: Two stores: hot location vs durable trip/money.
hints.2: DriverLocation in Redis; Fare/Ride in SQL; status machine.
hints.3: Redis: lat/lng/cell/status (+ GEO or H3 sets); SQL: Fare/Ride/users; statuses REQUESTED→…→COMPLETED/CANCELLED; optional Offer.

phases.goal: Wire Location, Ride, Matching/Dispatch, geo index, ETA, locks, and push behind a city-local control plane.

must_hit.point: Components: API Gateway → Ride Service (SQL Fare/Ride) → Matching/Dispatch using Geo Index (Redis GEO or H3 cells), ETA/Routing, and Lock (Redis TTL) / CAS on Driver; Location Service takes high-QPS GPS into Redis (+ Kafka analytics); Notification/Push (FCM/APNs/WS).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches Ride + Matching + Geo + ETA + Lock, separate Location Service, and push.

must_hit.point: Ping loop: Driver → Location Service → GEOADD / cell membership update (+ TTL / last-seen). Request: create REQUESTED → enqueue match job (Kafka/SQS) → ack rider.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Narrates GPS update into geo index and async match enqueue after REQUESTED.

must_hit.point: Match: geo candidates → filter status/vehicle → rank by ETA → lock driver → push offer → accept window → cascade or fail; trip status transitions in SQL while location stream continues for map UX.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks candidate→rank→lock→offer→cascade and SQL trip transitions with ongoing location.

must_hit.point: Shard by city/region: matching is almost always local; partition geo index + match workers by metro so hot cities don’t sink the globe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Partitions geo index and matchers by metro/city affinity.

probes: Draw the services for location updates and matching — what happens from ride request to driver offer?

hints.1: Separate Location firehose from Ride/Matching control plane.
hints.2: Request enqueues match; match uses geo → ETA → lock → push.
hints.3: Location→Redis GEO/H3; Ride creates REQUESTED→queue; match candidates→ETA rank→Redis TTL/CAS lock→offer→cascade; city-shard workers; push via FCM/APNs/WS.

phases.goal: Defend geo-index choice, greedy vs batch dispatch, assignment locks, and ETA ranking.

must_hit.point: Geo pattern: snap point → cell (geohash/H3) → query center + neighbors (geohash 3×3 or H3 gridDisk/k-ring) → refine with distance or road-network ETA; never scan the global fleet.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes cell + neighbor ring then refine, rejecting a global fleet scan.

must_hit.point: Redis GEO (geohash under the hood) is the fast interview nearby answer; H3 cell sets give uniform neighbor distance / near-equal area for dispatch + surge; PostGIS/quadtree alone is painful as sole store at ~10^4–10^5 writes/s.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Redis GEO vs H3 rings vs PostGIS/quadtree under high write rates.

must_hit.point: Greedy closest is low-latency and easy to cascade but locally suboptimal; batch marketplace waits 2–5s and bipartite-optimizes system ETAs for better network efficiency at harder ops cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts greedy cascade with 2–5s batched ETA optimization.

must_hit.point: Prevent double-dispatch with atomic reserve (UPDATE … WHERE status='AVAILABLE' or Redis lock + TTL ≈ accept window); location may be eventually consistent / slightly stale (seconds); assignment must be linearizable on the driver.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows CAS/lock+TTL unlock and the location-vs-assignment consistency split.

must_hit.point: ETA ≠ crow-flies: Haversine filters candidates; ranking uses routing + traffic; DeepETA is a residual ML refinement on a routing engine — don’t invent model details.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Filters with Haversine, ranks with routing/traffic, optionally names DeepETA without fake model math.

probes: Would you use Redis GEO or H3, greedy or batch matching, and how do you stop double-assigning a driver?

hints.1: Pick geo index and assignment consistency as the first deep dives.
hints.2: Cell+neighbors; then greedy vs 2–5s batch; then lock TTL.
hints.3: Geohash 3×3 or H3 k-ring→refine; Redis GEO vs H3 vs PostGIS at ~10^4–10^5 writes/s; batch 2–5s; CAS/Redis lock+TTL; Haversine filter, routing rank, optional DeepETA.

phases.goal: Scale the GPS firehose, hot cells, match storms, offer durability, and map-read amplification.

must_hit.point: GPS write firehose: shard Redis by city / H3 parent; adaptive ping rate (slow when parked); don’t persist every ping on the match path.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shards geo storage, slows parked pings, and keeps history off the match path.

must_hit.point: Hot downtown cells and match storms: finer H3 resolution or split GEO keys; more match workers on that city’s queue partition; expand k-ring/radius; surge to rebalance; degrade to longer ETA honestly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Splits hot cells, scales city matchers, expands search, and uses surge/honest ETA degrade.

must_hit.point: Offer timeouts: delay queue or durable workflow (Temporal/Cadence — Uber origin story) so crashes don’t lose REQUESTED rides; multi-region keeps active city affinity and local supply matching.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses durable match workflow for REQUESTED survival and city-affinity multi-region.

must_hit.point: Map read amplification: fuzz + throttle nearby queries; push location to the matched rider only after accept.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Throttles/fuzzes nearby and pushes precise location only post-accept.

probes: A stadium lets out — what melts first on location writes and matching, and how do you degrade?

hints.1: Think ping firehose and city queue before global capacity.
hints.2: Shard/adaptive pings; hot-cell splits; autoscale matchers + surge.
hints.3: City/H3 shard + slow parked pings; finer H3/split GEO; expand k-ring + surge; Temporal/Cadence for REQUESTED; fuzz/throttle nearby; push after accept.

tradeoffs.topic: Redis GEO vs H3 cell sets vs PostGIS/quadtree
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Redis GEO is the fastest interview nearby answer (geohash under the hood). H3 cell sets match Uber’s dispatch/surge story with uniform neighbor distance and near-equal area. PostGIS/quadtree alone is fine for static POIs but painful as the sole store at ~10^4–10^5 writes/s; quadtrees also mutate under heavy writes.

tradeoffs.topic: Greedy nearest offer vs batch dispatch
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Greedy closest is low latency and easy to cascade but can be locally suboptimal. Batch marketplace waits 2–5s, jointly optimizes open requests and drivers for system ETA / network efficiency, at higher operational complexity.

tradeoffs.topic: Location eventual consistency vs linearizable assignment
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Driver location can be slightly stale for a few seconds; assignment must be linearizable on the driver via atomic reserve (SQL CAS or Redis lock + TTL ≈ accept window) so two riders cannot keep the same driver.

Use crow-flies/Haversine only to filter candidates; rank with road-network routing and traffic. DeepETA is a residual ML layer on a routing engine — name it, don’t invent model details. Barriers (e.g. a river) make Haversine-closest wrong.

gotchas.trap: Using Postgres ORDER BY distance as the primary nearby query.
gotchas.correction: That tends toward a full scan / weak multi-dim B-tree path; geo-index first (cell + neighbors), then refine.

gotchas.trap: Two riders grab the same driver.
gotchas.correction: Show atomic CAS/lock on availability; the loser cascades to the next candidate.

gotchas.trap: Driver never responds and the rider blocks forever.
gotchas.correction: TTL unlock after the accept window and cascade; don’t wait indefinitely.

gotchas.trap: Picking the Haversine-closest driver stuck across a river.
gotchas.correction: ETA/routing beats crow-flies; talk barriers and road network.

gotchas.trap: Surge cliffs at cell edges / geohash borders.
gotchas.correction: Prefer H3 rings and neighbor blending so prices don’t cliff at borders.

gotchas.trap: Putting historical GPS trails on the match path or leaving offline drivers in the index.
gotchas.correction: Kafka → analytics/OLAP for history; Redis is current only; TTL / last-seen sweeper removes ghosts.
Security smell — server owns fare snapshots and driver identity via auth.
